blocks.heading: Key Concepts
blocks.html:
• Primary survey: ABCDE — Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure
  • Hypovolemic shock: loss of intravascular volume → inadequate tissue perfusion
  • Shock classes: I (<15%), II (15-30%), III (30-40%), IV (>40% blood loss)
  • Tension pneumothorax: one-way valve → increased intrapleural pressure → mediastinal shift
  • Cardiac tamponade: blood in pericardium → impaired ventricular filling → obstructive shock
  • Massive hemothorax: >1500 mL blood in hemithorax

blocks.heading: Normal Values
blocks.html:
• SBP >90 mmHg (until Class III shock)
  • HR <100 (Class I), 100-120 (II), 120-140 (III), >140 (IV)
  • MAP >65 mmHg (minimum for organ perfusion)
  • Urine output: 0.5-1 mL/kg/hr
  • Lactate <2 mmol/L

blocks.heading: What the Nurse Must Know
blocks.html:
• Tension pneumothorax: immediate needle decompression (2nd ICS, midclavicular line)
  • FAST exam: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma — evaluates pericardium, hepatorenal, splenorenal, suprapubic
  • Pelvic fracture: major source of occult blood loss — stabilize with binder
  • C-spine immobilization until cleared clinically and radiographically

blocks.heading: NORMAL FUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Intact airway, patent breathing
  • Stable hemodynamics, adequate perfusion
  • Intact CNS function
  • No active bleeding, no fractures

blocks.heading: DYSFUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Airway obstruction: tongue, blood, vomitus, foreign body
  • Tension pneumothorax: mediastinal shift, cardiovascular collapse
  • Hemorrhagic shock: blood loss → inadequate perfusion
  • Head injury: increased ICP, altered LOC
  • Spinal cord injury: neurogenic shock, paralysis

blocks.heading: ⚠ Risk Factors (Non-Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Male gender (higher trauma incidence)
  • Age extremes (pediatric, elderly)
  • Anticoagulant use (worsens bleeding)

blocks.heading: 💡 Risk Factors (Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Motor vehicle accidents (leading cause)
  • Falls (especially elderly)
  • Penetrating trauma (stab, gunshot)
  • Alcohol and drug intoxication
  • Occupational hazards
  • Violence and assault

blocks.heading: 🔥 Complications
blocks.html: Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) • Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) • Infection/sepsis • Permanent neurological deficit • Post-traumatic stress disorder
NRG Opposite: Trauma disrupts multiple systems → blood loss + organ damage → shock + disability

1. Mechanism of injury determines pattern: blunt vs penetrating

2. Primary injury: direct tissue damage at moment of impact

3. Hemorrhage: external or internal blood loss

4. Shock: inadequate tissue perfusion from hypovolemia

5. Secondary injury: hypoxia, hypotension, inflammation worsen primary damage

6. Systemic inflammatory response → MODS if uncontrolled

blocks.heading: Key Detail
blocks.html: Blunt trauma: MVC, falls, assault — causes shearing, compression, deceleration injuries. Penetrating trauma: stab, GSW — direct tissue disruption along wound track. Primary brain injury occurs at moment of impact; secondary injury (hypoxia, hypotension) is preventable and must be minimized. Damage control resuscitation: permissive hypotension, early blood products, prevent coagulopathy.

blocks.heading: Clinical Result
blocks.html: Hemorrhagic shock progresses through classes: Class I (<750 mL, 15%) — compensated; Class II (750-1500 mL, 15-30%) — tachycardia, anxiety; Class III (1500-2000 mL, 30-40%) — hypotension, confusion, oliguria; Class IV (>2000 mL, >40%) — profound hypotension, lethargy, anuria. Without intervention, progresses to irreversible shock and death.
NRG Sequencing: Each step leads to the next — understand the cascade to predict S/S and management

blocks.heading: Early / Mild
blocks.html:
• Tachycardia (first compensatory sign)
  • Anxiety, restlessness
  • Cool, clammy skin
  • Delayed capillary refill
  • Narrowed pulse pressure

blocks.heading: Severe
blocks.html:
• Hypotension (SBP <90)
  • Altered mental status (confusion, lethargy)
  • Tachypnea (compensatory)
  • Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr)
  • Pale, mottled skin

blocks.heading: Profound hypotension, unresponsive
blocks.html:
• Profound hypotension, unresponsive
  • Anuria
  • Coma (GCS <8)
  • Dilated fixed pupils (herniation)
  • THIS IS A MEDICAL EMERGENCY — Activate massive transfusion protocol

blocks.heading: Diagnostic / Assessment Findings
blocks.html:
• FAST exam: free fluid in peritoneum, pericardial effusion
  • CT scan: definitive imaging once stable
  • C-spine X-ray/CT: fracture/subluxation
  • Pelvis X-ray: fracture pattern
  • Chest X-ray: pneumothorax, hemothorax, widened mediastinum
  • ABG: acidosis, base deficit, lactate

blocks.heading: Link Patho to S/S
blocks.html:
Blood loss → Tachycardia, hypotension, cool clammy skin

Brain injury → Altered LOC, pupillary changes, focal deficits

Tension pneumothorax → Dyspnea, hypotension, tracheal deviation, JVD

Spinal cord injury → Neurogenic shock (warm dry skin, bradycardia), paralysis

blocks.heading: Cardiovascular
blocks.html:
• Carotid/femoral/radial pulses (absent = severe shock)
  • BP both arms (discrepancy = aortic dissection)
  • HR, rhythm
  • Capillary refill, skin color/temp
  • External bleeding control

blocks.heading: Respiratory
blocks.html:
• Airway patency (listen for stridor, gurgling)
  • Breathing rate, effort, symmetry
  • Tracheal deviation (tension pneumo)
  • Chest excursion
  • SpO2

blocks.heading: Neurological
blocks.html:
• GCS (E___V___M___ = total ___)
  • Pupil size and reaction
  • Lateralizing signs
  • Spinal assessment: motor/sensory level

blocks.heading: Key Laboratory & Diagnostic Tests
rows: May be normal initially (fluid shift takes time)

blocks.heading: Priority Actions
blocks.html: PRIMARY SURVEY — ABCDE: Airway with C-spine control, Breathing, Circulation (bleeding control, 2 large-bore IVs), Disability (GCS, pupils), Exposure (undress, prevent hypothermia). Control external hemorrhage with direct pressure. Pelvic binder if unstable pelvis. FAST exam. Do NOT get distracted by obvious injuries — life-threatening conditions first.

blocks.heading: 💊 Pharmacology - Nursing Monitoring
rows: 3:1 rule (3 mL crystalloid per 1 mL blood lost); beware of dilutional coagulopathy
Titrate carefully in hemodynamically unstable patients

blocks.heading: Hypothermia & TRIAD of Death Alert
blocks.html: Trauma TRIAD of death: Hypothermia + Acidosis + Coagulopathy — vicious cycle that worsens bleeding. Prevent hypothermia: warm fluids, blankets, ambient temperature >28°C. Do NOT over-resuscitate with crystalloids — causes hemodilution, edema, and compartment syndrome. Permissive hypotension (SBP 80-90) acceptable in penetrating trauma until definitive control.

blocks.heading: Lifestyle & Patient Education
blocks.html:
• Rehabilitation: physical, occupational, speech therapy
  • Psychological support: PTSD screening and treatment
  • Fall prevention strategies (elderly)
  • Road safety education
  • Violence prevention programs
🚨 Report Immediately: GCS <8 | SBP <90 | SpO2 <90% | Signs of herniation | Uncontrolled bleeding | Tension pneumothorax

blocks.heading: Nursing Diagnosis
blocks.html: Deficient fluid volume related to hemorrhage from multiple trauma as evidenced by SBP 78/52, HR 128, cool clammy skin, and lactate 4.8 mmol/L

blocks.heading: Goal / Outcome
blocks.html: Patient will achieve hemodynamic stability (SBP >90, HR <100, urine output >0.5 mL/kg/hr, lactate <2) within 4 hours of resuscitation.

blocks.heading: Interventions
blocks.html:
• Two large-bore IVs (14-16 gauge) or intraosseous access
  • Fluid resuscitation per protocol (crystalloid then blood products)
  • Apply warmed blankets, warm IV fluids
  • External hemorrhage control with direct pressure
  • Foley catheter for accurate urine output
  • Prepare for OR if hemodynamically unstable

blocks.heading: Rationale
blocks.html: Large-bore IVs allow rapid fluid administration. Warmed fluids prevent hypothermia (part of lethal triad). Direct pressure controls external bleeding. Urine output is the best indicator of end-organ perfusion. Unstable patients need definitive surgical control of bleeding.

blocks.heading: Evaluation
blocks.html: SBP 104/68, HR 96. Urine output 45 mL/hr. Lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Warm, dry skin. Patient transferred to OR for exploratory laparotomy.
NRG Care Plan Formula: Problem → Goal → Interventions → Rationale → Evaluation

What system is being tested?

Multi-System — trauma affects multiple body systems simultaneously

What is the priority?

ABCDE primary survey + C-spine + hemorrhage control + massive transfusion if needed

What is unsafe?

Getting distracted by obvious injuries, missing tension pneumothorax, over-resuscitating with crystalloids

What restores function?

Definitive hemorrhage control (OR/angio) + blood products + damage control resuscitation

blocks.heading: 💡 Key Memory Aids for RENR
blocks.html:
• ABCDE: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure — NEVER skip order
  • Tension pneumothorax: Immediate needle decompression 2nd ICS midclavicular — do NOT wait for X-ray
  • Lethal triad: Hypothermia + Acidosis + Coagulopathy — prevent at all costs
  • Tranexamic acid: 1 g IV within 3 hours of injury — reduces mortality from bleeding
  • Tachycardia FIRST: Tachycardia is the FIRST sign of shock — hypotension is a LATE sign
NRG System Focus Formula: Trauma → Multi-System → Hemorrhage + organ damage → Shock → Priority: ABCDE survey + hemorrhage control + massive transfusion

question.stem: A 35-year-old patient arrives in the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. The primary survey reveals: patent airway, bilateral breath sounds, HR 132, BP 82/50, RR 28, GCS 14. There is obvious deformity of the left thigh and abdominal distension. What is the nurse's priority intervention?

options.html: Splint the femur fracture and prepare for orthopedic surgery
Insert a nasogastric tube to decompress the abdomen
Establish two large-bore IVs and initiate fluid resuscitation with warmed crystalloids
Perform a focused abdominal ultrasound to identify the source of bleeding

question.rationale: The patient is in Class III hemorrhagic shock (HR 132, SBP 82/50, RR 28 compensatory) with multiple sources of blood loss (femur fracture can lose 1-2 L; abdominal distension suggests intra-abdominal bleeding). The priority is immediate large-bore IV access and fluid resuscitation. Femur fractures can lose 1-2 liters of blood into the thigh. Two large-bore IVs (14-16 gauge) allow rapid fluid administration. Option A (splinting) is important but does not address the life-threatening hemorrhage. Option B (NG tube) is not a priority in hemorrhagic shock. Option D (FAST exam) is important for diagnosis but should not delay resuscitation — resuscitate and examine simultaneously.

why.html: Splinting addresses the fracture but not the life-threatening hemorrhage
NG tube is not priority in hemorrhagic shock
FAST is diagnostic but should not delay resuscitation
